Run 3 (high S, high P) successfully penalized M7 (substrate-induced activation/inhibition) and separated the models into two main camps at the top of the leaderboard: catalyst activation models (M8, M6) and higher-order catalyst interaction models (M19, M2, M3), with standard Michaelis-Menten (M1) still closely trailing. My aim to isolate `catS` specific behaviors worked to penalize M16 and M17, but we now need a strategy to cleanly differentiate between pre-activation (M6/M8) and catalyst-catalyst interactions (M19/M2).
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To cleanly separate catalyst activation mechanisms (M6, M8) from catalyst-catalyst interaction mechanisms (M19, M2, M3), I propose an experiment in the extreme low-catalyst, high-substrate regime ([S]0 = 5.0, [cat]0 = 0.01, [P]0 = 0.0). 
1. By using a very low catalyst concentration (0.01), all second-order catalyst interactions (such as `2cat` dimerization in M2/M3 or `cat + catS` deactivation in M19) will be heavily suppressed. If one of these is the true model, the kinetic profile in this regime will collapse and look almost identical to standard Michaelis-Menten (M1).
2. Conversely, if a catalyst activation step is required (M6, M8), the low catalyst concentration will stretch out the overall reaction time. This will make any initial lag phase (due to slow `cat => cat*` conversion) highly visible over a long pseudo-zero-order regime. M1 cannot fit a lag phase, so this will perfectly isolate M6/M8.
3. Using [P]0 = 0.0 ensures the baseline is clean and any observed deviations early in the reaction are strictly due to catalyst activation dynamics, not product inhibition.
</hypothesis>
